definition: A subword tokenization method that iteratively merges the most frequent pair of symbols into a single token.
details: BPE starts with individual characters and repeatedly merges the most common adjacent pair, building a fixed-size vocabulary of character fragments. This lets a model handle rare and out-of-vocabulary words as sequences of known subwords, which is far more robust than whole-word vocabularies for morphologically rich languages.

explainer.lead: Byte-Pair Encoding, or BPE, breaks text into reusable pieces that sit between single characters and whole words. This gives a model a manageable vocabulary while still letting it read unfamiliar words instead of failing on them.

tiers.eli5: Imagine building words from small snap-together blocks instead of needing a special block for every possible word. BPE learns which neighboring letters appear together most often and joins them into bigger blocks. A strange new word can then be built from familiar smaller pieces.
tiers.practitioner: Train the merge rules on text, choose a target vocabulary size, and apply the learned rules consistently when tokenizing new input. The main trade-off is sequence length versus vocabulary coverage: rare words remain representable, but they may split into several tokens. Treat the resulting fragments as statistical units, not necessarily meaningful parts of words.
tiers.paperLevel: Given an initial character vocabulary V_0, repeatedly select (a,b) = arg max count(a,b) over adjacent symbol pairs, replace occurrences of that pair with ab, and set V_(t+1) = V_t union {ab}. Stop when the fixed target vocabulary size is reached. This handles rare and out-of-vocabulary words through known subwords, but merges reflect frequency rather than linguistic meaning and rare words can require longer token sequences.

explainer.example: Suppose 'low' is common and 'l o' is the most frequent pair: 'l o w' becomes 'lo w'. If 'lo w' later becomes the most frequent pair, it becomes the single token 'low'. The unfamiliar word 'below' can still be encoded as 'b e low' rather than requiring its own whole-word token.

explainer.intuition: Common character combinations deserve their own tokens, while uncommon words can still be assembled from smaller pieces. BPE discovers those combinations directly from how often neighboring symbols occur together.
howItWorks: Start with individual characters as the initial symbols.
Count every adjacent pair of symbols in the text.
Merge the most frequent pair into one new token.
Repeat the counting and merging until the vocabulary reaches its fixed size.
Encode later text using the learned characters and subword tokens.
explainer.whyItMatters: BPE keeps the vocabulary bounded without making unseen words unreadable. It is especially useful when language produces many rare or varied word forms that a whole-word vocabulary would miss.
misconceptions: BPE tokens are not guaranteed to match meaningful prefixes, roots, or suffixes.
BPE does not use an unlimited vocabulary; merging stops at a chosen fixed size.
An unfamiliar word is not necessarily one token; it may be split into several known pieces.
